claim: The structure of the intact functional assembly responsible for regulating and executing a site-specific DNA recombination reaction is a 240-bp Holliday junction (HJ) bound specifically by 11 protein subunits.
source: The assembly is a 240-bp Holliday junction (HJ) bound specifically by 11 protein subunits.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by the cryo-EM structure determination described in the manuscript.

claim: The higher-order complex is a key intermediate in the tightly regulated pathway for the excision of bacteriophage λ viral DNA out of the E. coli host chromosome.
source: This higher-order complex is a key intermediate in the tightly regulated pathway for the excision of bacteriophage λ viral DNA out of the E. coli host chromosome, an extensively studied paradigmatic model system for the regulated rearrangement of DNA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental characterization of the excisive HJ complex.

claim: The site-specific recombinase (Int) encoded by bacteriophage λ is the archetypical member of the tyrosine recombinase family.
source: The site-specific recombinase (Int) encoded by bacteriophage λ is the archetypical member of the tyrosine recombinase family, whose members carry out such diverse functions as chromosome segregation, chromosome copy number control, gene expression, conjugative transposition, gene dissemination, and viral integration and excision (Craig et al., 2015; Jayaram et al., 2015; Landy, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to review articles.

claim: All tyrosine recombinases use the same isoenergetic phosphoryl transfer chemistry and sequential strand exchange mechanism to execute DNA rearrangements via the formation and resolution of a transient four-way DNA junction, or Holliday junction (HJ), recombination intermediate.
source: All tyrosine recombinases use the same isoenergetic phosphoryl transfer chemistry and sequential strand exchange mechanism to execute DNA rearrangements via the formation and resolution of a transient four-way DNA junction, or Holliday junction (HJ), recombination intermediate (Hsu and Landy, 1984; Kitts and Nash, 1988a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to primary research articles.

claim: In contrast to Cre and FLP, where the entire bidirectional recombination reaction is executed by a recombinase tetramer, Int carries out two opposing reactions that are both highly directional and tightly regulated.
source: In contrast to two other well-studied and highly exploited family members, Cre and FLP, where the entire bidirectional recombination reaction is executed by a recombinase tetramer (Jayaram et al., 2015; Van Duyne, 2015), Int carries out two opposing reactions that are both highly directional and tightly regulated.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Each Int reaction requires the assembly of a unique 400 kDa multi-protein complex using accessory DNA-bending proteins and an overlapping ensemble of accessory binding sites.
source: Each reaction requires the assembly of a unique 400 kDa multi-protein complex using accessory DNA-bending proteins and an overlapping ensemble of accessory binding sites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with the structural data presented.

claim: Integrative recombination requires the virally-encoded integrase protein (Int) and the bacterial accessory protein Integration Host Factor (IHF).
source: The integrative reaction requires the virally-encoded integrase protein (Int) and the bacterial accessory protein Integration Host Factor (IHF).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 legend and is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The excisive reaction additionally requires the virally encoded accessory protein Xis (which also inhibits the integrative reactions).
source: The excisive reaction additionally requires the virally encoded accessory protein Xis (which also inhibits the integrative reactions).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 legend and is supported by the structural data showing Xis in the excisive complex.

claim: Both integrative and excisive reactions are stimulated by the bacterial accessory protein Fis.
source: Both reactions are stimulated by the bacterial accessory protein Fis.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 legend and supported by citations.

claim: Both integrative and excisive reactions proceed through a four-way DNA junction called a Holliday junction (HJ).
source: Both reactions proceed through a four-way DNA junction called a Holliday junction (HJ) (see Panel B for details of these DNA strand exchanges) (reviewed in [Landy, 2015]).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1 legend and supported by citations and the structural data.

claim: Cutting, recombining, and resealing DNA during recombination proceeds by two pairs of sequential single-strand DNA exchanges that are staggered by seven base pairs.
source: Cutting, recombining, and resealing DNA during recombination proceeds by two pairs of sequential single-strand DNA exchanges that are staggered by seven base pairs that are identical in all four att sites; they are referred to as the 'overlap' region (O).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1B legend and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: The molecular details of λ Int recombination are common to all reactions catalyzed by the large family of tyrosine recombinases.
source: The molecular details of this recombination are common to all reactions catalyzed by the large family of tyrosine recombinases (except for the size of the O regions and the order of strand exchanges), as first characterized for λ Int, Cre, Flp, and XerC/D (reviewed in [Van Duyne, 2015]).
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1B legend and supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The recombination proceeds in the absence of exogenous energy via the formation of high-energy covalent 3'phospho-tyrosine intermediates in the active site of each Int protein.
source: It proceeds in the absence of exogenous energy via the formation of high-energy covalent 3'phospho-tyrosine intermediates in the active site of each Int protein.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1B legend and is supported by established knowledge of tyrosine recombinase mechanism.

claim: The first pair of strand exchanges during integrative recombination always occurs at the C and B core sites.
source: The first pair of exchanges, always at the C (green) and B (blue) core sites, is initiated by formation of 3' phospho-tyrosine linkages (with Tyr342) and 5' OH termini.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1B legend and is supported by established mechanistic knowledge.

claim: Int is a heterobivalent DNA binding protein that binds to high affinity 'arm-type' DNA sites via its small amino-terminal domain (NTD) and more weakly to 'core-type' DNA sites.
source: Int is a heterobivalent DNA binding protein that binds to high affinity 'arm-type' DNA sites via its small amino-terminal domain (NTD) and more weakly to 'core-type' DNA sites, where DNA cleavage and ligation take place.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by structural and biochemical data.

claim: Int binds to core sites via a central core binding domain (CB) and a C-terminal catalytic domain (CAT).
source: Int binds to core sites via a central core binding domain (CB) and a C-terminal catalytic domain (CAT); the latter two domains are referred to here as the CTD (see Figure 2; Moitoso et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The Int subunits within a recombinogenic complex bind and bridge arm- and core-type DNA sites in patterns determined by the accessory DNA bending proteins IHF, Xis, and Fis.
source: The Int subunits within a recombinogenic complex bind and bridge arm- and core-type DNA sites in patterns determined by the accessory DNA bending proteins IHF, Xis, and Fis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Differential occupancy of the 16 protein binding sites on the 240 bp att site generates two overlapping ensembles that differentiate the integrative and excisive recombination pathways.
source: Differential occupancy of the 16 protein binding sites on the 240 bp att site generates two overlapping ensembles that differentiate the integrative and excisive recombination pathways ([Seah et al., 2014; Tong et al., 2014]; (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The structure of the excisive complex was determined at 11 Å resolution using single particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM).
source: Using techniques described previously (Figure 3), we trapped and purified the multi-protein HJ complex of excisive recombination and determined its structure at 11 Å resolution using single particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the detailed methods and results sections.

claim: Stable HJ complexes were trapped by in vitro recombination between attL and attR partners whose respective seven bp overlap sequences were designed to generate a fully paired HJ overlap sequence that would create mismatched base pairs upon reversal or progression of the recombination reaction.
source: Stable HJ complexes were trapped by in vitro recombination between attL and attR partners whose respective seven bp overlap sequences were designed to generate a fully paired HJ overlap sequence that would create mismatched base pairs upon reversal or progression of the recombination reaction (Matovina et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 66,033 particles were selected from 1359 images for cryo-EM analysis.
source: We selected 66,033 particles from 1359 images (for example, Figure 3B) and obtained two-dimensional (2D) class averages using the ISAC procedure (Yang et al., 2012) after pixel binning (effective pixel size 5.6 Å).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: Only 17% of the particles ended up in the final reconstruction due to substantial heterogeneity of the sample.
source: Due to the substantial heterogeneity of the sample – only 17% of the particles ended up in the final reconstruction (Figure 3D) – we performed six such refinement/classification rounds, always initializing the next round with the reconstruction of the previous round that had the highest average particle score.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The final map contained 10,956 particles and reached a resolution of about 11 Å.
source: The best reconstruction contained 10,956 particles and reached a resolution of about 11 Å (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FSC analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At the center of the excisive complex an integrase tetramer is bound to a core-site HJ, where strand exchange has taken place between the B half-site of attL and the C half-site of attR.
source: At the center of the excisive complex an integrase tetramer is bound to a core-site HJ, where strand exchange has taken place between the B half-site of attL and the C half-site of attR (see Figures 1B and 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the overall structure and is supported by the structural model.

claim: The most striking features of the complex are the tight bends of the P and P' arms as they emerge from the C and C' core half-sites.
source: The most striking features of the complex are the tight bends of the P and P' arms as they emerge from the C and C' core half-sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is visible in the structural models shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: IHF heterodimers bend the P arm at the H2 site and the P' arm at the H' site, in each case re-directing the DNA back towards the Int tetramer.
source: IHF heterodimers bend the P arm at the H2 site and the P' arm at the H' site, in each case re-directing the DNA back towards the Int tetramer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is visible in the structural models shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: For P', the IHF bend is sufficient for the P'1 and P'2 arm-binding sites to be engaged by the Int subunits bound at the C' and B core sites, respectively.
source: For P', the IHF bend is sufficient for the P'1 and P'2 arm-binding sites to be engaged by the Int subunits bound at the C' and B core sites, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is visible in Figure 6B.

claim: Three Xis subunits provide a second change in direction of the P arm, directing it across the top of the Int tetramer.
source: Three Xis subunits provide a second change in direction of the P arm, directing it across the top of the Int tetramer (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is visible in Figure 6A.

claim: The DNA bend observed in the Xis•DNA crystal structure fits well into the EM envelope.
source: Remarkably, the DNA bend observed in the Xis•DNA crystal structure (Abbani et al., 2007) fits well into the EM envelope, which has strong density for both the DNA and the Xis subunits.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrates agreement between the EM structure and previous crystal structures.

claim: Fis was not present in the complexes analyzed by EM.
source: Fis was not present in the complexes analyzed by EM and as expected, there is no density corresponding to Fis at this site.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is consistent with the sample preparation.

claim: Fis can be readily accommodated by the structure.
source: We note, however that Fis can be readily accommodated by the structure (Figure 6C), which fits well with the proposed role for Fis as a non-essential enhancer of recombination (Ball and Johnson, 1991a; 1991b; Esposito and Gerard, 2003; Thompson et al., 1987a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by modeling and citations.

claim: The NTD of Int-C has no known function in excisive recombination, since only three arm-binding sites are used in the reaction.
source: This domain has no known function in excisive recombination, since only three arm-binding sites are used in the reaction (Numrych et al., 1990; Thompson et al., 1987b; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The overall architecture of the EM structure is in broad agreement with the FRET-based model.
source: The overall architecture of our EM structure is in broad agreement with the FRET-based model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the EM structure to previous FRET data.

claim: The tight, parallel paths of the P and P' arms were not predicted in the FRET model.
source: For example, the tight, parallel paths of the P and P' arms were not predicted in the FRET model, nor was the extensive Xis-Int interface that links the two arms together (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the EM structure to previous FRET data.

claim: There is excellent agreement between the EM structure and the FRET distance estimates for those dye positions that were correctly predicted to be free from steric interference.
source: Thus, there is excellent agreement between the EM structure and the FRET distance estimates for those dye positions that were correctly predicted to be free from steric interference.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the distance comparisons in Table 1.

claim: In crystal structures of Int complexes containing simplified oligonucleotide arm-binding sites, the DNA bound by Int NTDs lies parallel to the Int tetramer and the Int NTD-CB linkers form a compact network of interactions.
source: In crystal structures of Int complexes containing simplified oligonucleotide arm-binding sites, the DNA bound by Int NTDs lies parallel to the Int tetramer and the Int NTD-CB linkers form a compact network of interactions (Biswas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to a crystal structure.

claim: In the EM structure, the P' arm follows a relatively straight path after the H' bend, resulting in an upwards trajectory as it passes over the Int tetramer.
source: In contrast, the P' arm in the EM structure follows a relatively straight path after the H' bend, resulting in an upwards trajectory as it passes over the Int tetramer (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is visible in Figure 6B.

claim: Int-C' and Int-B linkers must adopt extended and distinct conformations in order to bridge the P' arm and the Int CB domains.
source: Consequently, Int-C' and Int-B linkers must adopt extended and distinct conformations in order to bridge the P' arm and the Int CB domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural model.

claim: Int bridge formation at P'1 and P'2 of attL does not require bending of the P' arm after the IHF-directed U-turn at H'.
source: Int bridge formation at P'1 and P'2 of attL therefore does not require bending of the P' arm after the IHF-directed U-turn at H'.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural model.

claim: Int uses the inherent flexibility present in the NTD-CB linker regions to reach the P'1 and P'2 binding sites.
source: Instead, Int uses the inherent flexibility present in the NTD-CB linker regions to reach the P'1 and P'2 binding sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural model.

claim: A primary function of Xis is to bend the P arm to stabilize a synapsis-competent attR complex.
source: A primary function of Xis is to bend the P arm to stabilize a synapsis-competent attR complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by the structural data.

claim: Xis mediates a substantial protein-protein interface between the P and P' arms.
source: The EM structure reveals that Xis also mediates a substantial protein-protein interface between the P and P' arms.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is visible in Figure 6C.

claim: The Xis molecules bound at the X1 and X1.5 sites of the P arm are packed against the Int-B and Int-C' NTDs bound at the P'2 and P'1 sites, respectively.
source: The Xis molecules bound at the X1 and X1.5 sites of the P arm are packed against the Int-B and Int-C' NTDs bound at the P'2 and P'1 sites, respectively (Figure 6C and Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is visible in Figure 6C.

claim: The Xis1.5-Int-C' interface appears to be particularly extensive.
source: The Xis1.5-Int-C' interface appears to be particularly extensive, although at the resolution of the EM density, we cannot visualize the conformations or roles of individual side chains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the EM density.

claim: The Xis-mediated interface between the P and P' arms provides an explanation for how synapsis is facilitated in the excisive pathway.
source: The identification of a Xis-mediated interface between the P and P' arms provides an explanation for how synapsis is facilitated in the excisive pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the structural data.

claim: Int binds only weakly to the core sites of attL and attR and the Int-bound core sites do not form stable synaptic complexes that undergo recombination.
source: Int binds only weakly to the core sites of attL and attR and the Int-bound core sites do not form stable synaptic complexes that undergo recombination (Bushman et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The three Int NTDs in the excisive complex are arranged in a linear manner, where the NTD bound at P2 makes no contact with the NTDs bound at P'1 or P'2.
source: The three Int NTDs in the excisive complex are arranged in a linear manner, where the NTD bound at P2 makes no contact with the NTDs bound at P'1 or P'2 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is visible in Figure 6C.

claim: Xis-NTD, and possibly Xis-linker interactions provide the additional glue required to hold attL and attR together and allow the initial strand exchange to take place.
source: Instead, Xis-NTD, and possibly Xis-linker interactions provide the additional glue required to hold attL and attR together and allow the initial strand exchange to take place.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the structural data.

claim: There are 18 residues at the C-terminus of Xis that were missing in the Xis•DNA crystal structures and are not included in the excisive complex model.
source: There are 18 residues at the C-terminus of Xis that were missing in the Xis•DNA crystal structures (Abbani et al., 2007; Sam et al., 2004) and are not included in our excisive complex model.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: Six of the eighteen missing C-terminal residues of Xis are arginine or lysine, suggesting that the basic C-terminal tails of Xis could interact with P and/or P' arm DNA.
source: Six of the eighteen missing residues are arginine or lysine, suggesting that the basic C-terminal tails of Xis could interact with P and/or P' arm DNA, further stabilizing a synaptic interface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on speculation about the missing residues.

claim: The C-terminus of Xis bound at X1 is directed at the Int-B NTD bound at P2, consistent with the observed cooperativity of Xis and Int binding to attR arm DNA.
source: The C-terminus of Xis bound at X1 is instead directed at the Int-B NTD bound at P2, consistent with the observed cooperativity of Xis and Int binding to attR arm DNA (Bushman et al., 1985; Numrych et al., 1992; Sarkar et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The EM structure reveals three functional roles for Xis in excisive recombination: promoting Int NTD binding at the weak P2 site; bending the P arm to place P2 in position for cooperative Int binding and formation of a synapsis-competent attR; mediating an Xis•Int interface between the P and P' arms that facilitates attL x attR synapsis.
source: Thus, the EM structure reveals and/or explains three functional roles for Xis in excisive recombination: i) promoting Int NTD binding at the weak P2 site; ii) bending the P arm to place P2 in position for cooperative Int binding and formation of a synapsis-competent attR; iii) mediating an Xis•Int interface between the P and P' arms that facilitates attL x attR synapsis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural data and inference.

claim: Fis is not required for excisive recombination, but it does stimulate the reaction when Xis is limiting.
source: Although Fis is not required for excisive recombination, it does stimulate the reaction when Xis is limiting (Thompson et al., 1987a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Fis binding stabilizes the A-tract bend in attR and facilitates Xis binding.
source: Fis binding stabilizes the A-tract bend in attR (Stella et al., 2010) and facilitates Xis binding (Papagiannis et al., 2007), providing additional sources of cooperativity for P arm assembly that would enhance the activity of Xis at lower concentrations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The scissile phosphodiesters, which flank the 7-bp crossover sequence located at the center of the core sites, form a parallelogram in the HJ intermediate.
source: The scissile phosphodiesters, which flank the 7-bp crossover sequence located at the center of the core sites, form a parallelogram in the HJ intermediate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural model.

claim: The sites that are active for cleavage form the closer diagonal pair in the scissile phosphate parallelogram; those that are inactive are farther apart.
source: The sites that are active for cleavage form the closer diagonal pair; those that are inactive are farther apart.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural model.

claim: Isomerization of the HJ intermediate between a top-strand cleavage configuration and a bottom-strand cleavage configuration involves exchanging angles within the scissile phosphate parallelogram.
source: Isomerization of the HJ intermediate between a top-strand cleavage configuration and a bottom-strand cleavage configuration involves exchanging angles within the scissile phosphate parallelogram (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: In the Cre system, isomerization is coupled to changes in the angles between the core site duplexes that converge at the center of the junction.
source: In the Cre system, isomerization is coupled to changes in the angles between the core site duplexes that converge at the center of the junction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on knowledge of the Cre system.

claim: Changes in the interfaces between catalytic domain subunits that result from isomerization are responsible for activation/deactivation of active site pairs in Cre.
source: Changes in the interfaces between catalytic domain subunits that result from isomerization are responsible for activation/deactivation of active site pairs (Van Duyne, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The core HJ isomer fit in the EM structure corresponds to a bottom strand cleavage configuration, where the complex is poised to carry out strand exchange to form attP and attB products.
source: The core HJ isomer that we fit in the EM structure corresponds to a bottom strand cleavage configuration, where the complex is poised to carry out strand exchange to form attP and attB products (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural model.

claim: Although there are significant changes near the center of the core complex where the HJ branch migrates by one bp during isomerization, the ends of the duplexes remain essentially in the same position, with only small torsional changes.
source: Although there are significant changes near the center of the core complex where the HJ branch migrates by one bp, the ends of the duplexes remain essentially in the same position, with only small torsional changes (Figure 7 and Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on modeling of the alternative isomer.

claim: At the resolution of the EM data, the two HJ isomers cannot be distinguished and the complexes analyzed may be a mixture of the two isomeric forms.
source: Thus, at the resolution of our EM data, we cannot distinguish between HJ isomers and the complexes analyzed may be a mixture of the two isomeric forms.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the resolution limitations of the EM data.

claim: Isomerization of the HJ intermediate can occur in the absence of large changes in quaternary structure and therefore does not require coupling to large changes in the P and P' arm positions.
source: In other words, the EM structure implies that isomerization of the HJ intermediate can occur in the absence of large changes in quaternary structure and therefore does not require coupling to large changes in the P and P' arm positions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the structural model.

claim: Small changes in position and torsion of the C and C' core sites can be accommodated by the in-plane and out of plane bending modes of IHF, with little impact on the Xis•Int interface assembled between the P and P' arms.
source: We suggest that small changes in position and torsion of the C and C' core sites can be accommodated by the in-plane and out of plane bending modes of IHF, with little impact on the Xis•Int interface assembled between the P and P' arms as they cross the Int tetramer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The odd-numbered 7-bp crossover region found in essentially all tyrosine integrases may facilitate isosteric isomerization.
source: This type of overall isosteric isomerization may be facilitated by the odd-numbered 7-bp crossover region that is found in essentially all tyrosine integrases, e.g. (Hakimi and Scocca, 1996; Kolot and Yagil, 1994; Peña et al., 1996; Williams, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The integrative HJ intermediate is formed when a complex containing attP DNA, an Int tetramer, and three IHF heterodimers captures the attB site in the host genome and carries out top strand exchange between the core DNA sequences.
source: The integrative HJ intermediate is formed when a complex containing attP DNA, an Int tetramer, and three IHF heterodimers captures the attB site in the host genome and carries out top strand exchange between the core DNA sequences (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on established knowledge.

claim: In both the integrative and excisive complexes, IHF bending at the H' site directs the P' arm over the CB domains of the Int tetramer.
source: In both the integrative and excisive complexes, IHF bending at the H' site directs the P' arm over the CB domains of the Int tetramer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the structural models.

claim: In the integrative complex, the B'-NTD binds at P'3, since Xis is not present to position the P2 site to bind to this domain.
source: In the integrative complex, the B'-NTD binds at P'3, since Xis is not present to position the P2 site to bind to this domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the integrative model.

claim: The P' arm trajectory requires no positional changes in order to readily accommodate binding of the C', C, and B' NTDs of Int in the integrative complex.
source: A striking aspect of the new integrative complex model is that the P' arm trajectory requires no positional changes in order to readily accommodate binding of the C', C, and B' NTDs of Int (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the integrative model.

claim: The P' arm position and trajectory appear to be invariant in excisive and integrative recombination.
source: Thus, the P' arm position and trajectory appear to be invariant in excisive and integrative recombination.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on comparison of the excisive and integrative models.

claim: In the absence of Xis, the P arm is not directed towards the Int NTDs after the H2 bend.
source: In the absence of Xis, the P arm is not directed towards the Int NTDs after the H2 bend.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the integrative model.

claim: IHF binding at the H1 site reverses the course of the P arm and directs it back towards the Int tetramer in the integrative complex.
source: Instead, it follows an upward trajectory beyond the P' arm, where IHF binding at the H1 site reverses its course and directs it back towards the Int tetramer (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on the integrative model.

claim: The P arm trajectory in the integrative complex places the P1 site within reach of the Int B-NTD, a high-affinity interaction that is crucial for integrative recombination.
source: This P arm trajectory places the P1 site within reach of the Int B-NTD, a high-affinity interaction that is crucial for integrative recombination (Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The P arm crosses the P' arm to position Int-B during integration, but runs parallel to the P' arm and promotes Int-B' binding at P2 during excision.
source: Thus, the P arm crosses the P' arm to position Int-B during integration, but runs parallel to the P' arm and promotes Int-B' binding at P2 during excision.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on comparison of the excisive and integrative models.

claim: The P-P' arm crossing that occurs during integration generates a negative DNA-crossing node.
source: The P-P' arm crossing that occurs during integration generates a negative DNA-crossing node, a feature that provides a structural explanation for the long-standing puzzle of why the topologies of integrative and excisive recombination are different and why supercoiling is required for efficient integration (Nash, 1975; Richet et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The integrative model cannot be constructed based on IHF-phased bends at H2 and H1 alone; additional DNA-bending is required.
source: Indeed, the integrative model shown in Figure 8 cannot be constructed based on IHF-phased bends at H2 and H1 alone; additional DNA-bending is required, which we suggest would occur naturally in a negatively supercoiled attP, but would be energetically unfavorable in linear substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on modeling.

claim: The P-P' crossing involves close DNA-DNA contacts between the arms, explaining in part the important role of polyamines such as spermidine and/or divalent cations in the integrative reaction.
source: The P-P' crossing also involves close DNA-DNA contacts between the arms, explaining in part the important role of polyamines such as spermidine and/or divalent cations in the integrative reaction (Kikuchi and Nash, 1978; Nash, 1975).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Both integrative and excisive recombination reactions are initiated by exchange of the same ('top') strands to form their respective HJ intermediates.
source: The biochemical feature defining excisive and integrative recombination as two different pathways (and not the forward and reverse of a single pathway) is the fact that both reactions are initiated by exchange of the same ('top') strands to form their respective HJ intermediates (Kitts and Nash, 1988b; Nunes-Düby et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: The order of strand exchange in both pathways is determined prior to synapsis by the patterns of specific Int bridges between arm and core sites and by the IHF- and Xis-induced bends that enable those bridges.

claim: The integrative complex model has an inherently flexible P arm which can transiently swing out along with Int bound at P1 to provide the dynamic binding required to embrace the bacterial chromosome and clasp onto a synapsed attB.
source: The integrative complex model shown in Figure 8 has an inherently flexible P arm which we propose can transiently swing out along with Int bound at P1 (Figure 9Ib). This would provide the dynamic binding required to embrace the bacterial chromosome and clasp onto a synapsed attB (Figure 9Ic), a structural feature that is consistent with genetic and biochemical results (Tong et al., 2014) and the especially high affinity of Int NTD for the P1 site (Sarkar et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on speculation and inference from the structural model, supported by citations.
